reviewEvidence.visualReviewMethod: Full-duration six-second contact sheets, English burned-in explanations, attack/recovery timelines and cancellation examples inspected; not continuous audio or every-frame review.
reviewEvidence.resolutionNote: Research-only reference media; never a production source. Independent production footage still requires genuine FHD or higher.

centralQuestion: Why does the movement after a strike contribute so much to the attack's impact?
thesis: A responsive attack may make contact quickly yet spend much longer in recovery. That visible follow-through must keep expressing the completed action, while its return-to-control pose agrees with the gameplay's cancellation timing.

claims: Follow-through is the movement after the attack, associated here with its recovery period.
Although it occurs after the hit, it is a substantial and memorable part of what the player sees.
sections.observedVisuals: Link's follow-through pose from the attack-breakdown lesson establishes the phase.
exampleRoles: A held post-strike pose identifies which portion is being discussed.
additionalPrerequisites: Distinguish the visible follow-through, the time the hit can register, and the gameplay recovery that restricts another action.
sections.ownScreenProposal: On the same Unity grid, show input, contact and follow-through on one timeline; keep the character fully visible and the recovery section highlighted.
sections.transitionToNext: Once the phase is identifiable, its length follows from the competing needs of quick response and meaningful vulnerability.

sections.role: Explain why the post-attack interval is long
claims: Smash attacks move rapidly from input through lead-in to attack to feel responsive.
Stronger attacks also need proportionate vulnerability afterward for back-and-forth play.
In the source's Smash examples, many normal and smash attacks finish in roughly a second or less, while contact often occurs in the first quarter to third, sometimes first fifth, of the action.
This leaves a large portion of the action after the initial strike.
sections.observedVisuals: Palutena, Bowser Jr., Ness, Captain Falcon, Ganondorf, Pac-Man and Wolf demonstrate fast strikes with visible recovery.
sections.retainedTeaching: Keep the response-versus-vulnerability reason and relative-time comparison. The approximate ratios describe this source's examples, not every game or a required design constant.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Demonstrate our own labelled 60-frame action with contact at frame 15, then keep counting through recovery. Mark these as illustrative authored timings; 15/60 = 0.25 seconds at 60 fps is a worked example, not measured Smash data.
sections.transitionToNext: The relative-time statement becomes concrete when several attacks are laid against the same input/contact/recovery markers.

claims: Different attacks have different timings, but their post-contact interval remains a major visible component.
Start, attack registration and recovery end must be distinguishable on the timeline.
sections.observedVisuals: Grid-isolated Mario, Marth, Ike, Rosalina & Luma, Donkey Kong, Diddy Kong, R.O.B., Toon Link, Mii Gunner, Villager, Little Mac and Palutena animations; frame counters and colour-coded timing bars identify registration and recovery.
exampleRoles: Fast and slower strikes test the same timing argument across movement types.
Weapon, body and projectile-style poses show that the meaningful post-attack pose varies with the action.
sections.retainedTeaching: Retain the comparative timing-gallery role with narrated action/results. Do not copy the finished grid montage or mechanically retain its music-led duration. Any narrower demonstration set must preserve the timing contrast and explain its selection.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Use the licensed rig on a fixed grid for a jab, heavy swing and projectile gesture, alongside independently obtained actual-game confirmation. Show only timings measured from our authored animation or independently verified gameplay.
sections.transitionToNext: The timeline's end marker needs a precise definition because the character can regain control before its visible animation has completely ended.

claims: The source highlights recovery end because cancel frames can permit the next action before visual return to standby.
Active hit windows are another component; the gallery is not a complete hitbox-data account.
sections.observedVisuals: Presenter clarifies cancel frames and active windows after the gallery.
sections.retainedTeaching: Do not label every post-registration frame as inactive, or confuse visual clip length with control lockout.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Add separate visible animation, active window and control-available tracks to the existing timeline, without inventing any real game's exact data.
sections.transitionToNext: With the intervals separated, return to what that long visible movement communicates.

sections.role: The follow-through must describe the attack
claims: The initial impact can be very brief while the aftermath occupies much more viewing time.
A follow-through should make it clear what the character just did.
Simply interpolating back to the idle pose wastes that expression.
Use the available follow-through time and clear movement to sustain the attack's character.
sections.observedVisuals: Ice Climbers' hammer swing, Wario and Rosalina illustrate held or expressive post-attack movement.
additionalPrerequisites: Introduce interpolation as generating the intermediate poses between two chosen poses before showing why a generic return can weaken the action.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Same rig, same contact and total timing: generic straight return versus expressive recovery. Show the residual direction of the hammer/body and let the viewer identify the action from the aftermath.
sections.transitionToNext: The expressive pose must still tell the truth about when the next input will work.

sections.role: Align visual recovery with restored control
claims: Assign cancel frames within the return toward standby where appropriate.
The pose at that time should look sufficiently recovered that receiving control feels expected.
Balance prolonged expression against the pose that signals readiness.
sections.observedVisuals: Inkling, Dr. Mario and Ike recovery examples accompany the cancel-frame explanation.
sections.ownScreenProposal: At one marked cancel frame, compare a still-committed body pose with a ready pose; trigger the same next movement to reveal why the latter transition is easier to understand.
sections.transitionToNext: The attack now reads as one continuous expressive action through its final controllable transition.

claims: The follow-through helps determine the impact of the whole attack.
Maintain clear expression through the ending instead of letting the action lose energy after contact.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Replay the complete improved attack once at native timing on the same grid, retaining the contact/recovery markers rather than resetting to a text-only ending.
